title: Let the market teach you what it is becoming.
dek: In Chapter 7 of The Innovator's Dilemma, Clayton Christensen explains why emerging markets cannot be forecast like established ones. The customer, product, and market must be discovered together through learning.

marginNote.label: Apprenticeship Note
marginNote.body: When the market does not yet exist, replace the demand forecast with a learning loop. Find the customers, applications, and product shape together before asking the plan to pretend they are known.

canon.heading: Discover the market before you scale the plan.
canon.standfirst: Read Chapter 7, "Discovering New and Emerging Markets," from Clayton M. Christensen's The Innovator's Dilemma on PDF pages 196-215. Christensen shows why disruptive markets are unknowable at the outset: suppliers and customers discover the application, product, and market together.
canon.readerIntro: Read this chapter as a warning against importing mature-market planning into an emerging market. Mark where Christensen replaces prediction with discovery, where customers reveal the product's real use, and where an early failure teaches the team what the market is not. Then write one discovery brief: target customer, job to be done, first use case, learning experiment, and evidence that would change the product.

blocks.label: 01 / Emerging markets cannot be analyzed in advance
paragraphs: A market that does not yet exist cannot be described with the same confidence as an established one. The relevant customers, applications, and dimensions of performance are still being formed.
The strategy therefore has to be a plan for learning and discovery. It cannot be a detailed execution plan built on assumptions that the market itself has not validated.

blocks.label: 02 / Customers and suppliers discover together
paragraphs: In a disruptive market, customers often cannot specify the product they need because they have not yet experienced the new possibility. Suppliers learn what to build by placing imperfect solutions in real contexts and observing what becomes useful.
The early product is not only a delivery mechanism. It is an instrument for discovering the customer's job, the valued outcome, and the market's actual boundaries.

blocks.label: 03 / Early applications reveal the market
paragraphs: The first viable use may not resemble the large market eventually imagined. An application that looks small or peripheral can reveal the performance tradeoff, customer, or workflow that makes the technology meaningful.
Treat those applications as evidence about the market rather than forcing them to satisfy a forecast made for a different one.

blocks.label: 04 / Learning changes the product definition
paragraphs: Because the market is discovered through use, product strategy must remain responsive to what customers do with the technology. The team learns not only whether demand exists, but what the product is actually for.
This is why disruptive innovation requires patience with ambiguity: premature certainty can close off the very observations that would define the opportunity.

blocks.label: 05 / Build a discovery loop before a scale plan
paragraphs: The practical assignment is to name the customer, job, first application, and experiment that can produce the next piece of market knowledge. The goal is not to predict the final market; it is to make the next uncertainty testable.
Stop with one emerging-market discovery brief: current assumption, smallest useful experiment, evidence to watch, and the product or customer definition that would change if the evidence disagrees.

closeReading: Why does Christensen say an emerging market is unknowable rather than merely difficult to forecast?
What do customers and suppliers have to discover together, and how does that change the role of the first product?
Which early application could reveal a market that a mature-market forecast would overlook?
Choose one emerging technology. What customer, job, and use case would you test first?
Write a discovery brief with one assumption, one learning experiment, and the evidence that would change your product definition.

principle.heading: Make the next market fact discoverable.
principle.body: When customers and applications are still forming, strategy should organize learning rather than simulate certainty. Use small experiments to discover what the market values before scaling the plan.
principle.example: A software company exploring an AI workflow should begin with one narrow team and one recurring job, observe where the tool changes behavior, and let those observations define the product before forecasting a category-sized market.
principle.practice: Choose one emerging opportunity. Write the current customer and use-case assumption, the smallest experiment that can test it, the behavior you will observe, and the product decision that follows from each possible result.

output.heading: Replace the forecast with a learning loop.
output.body: Find the smallest real use that can teach you who the customer is, what the product is for, and which market is beginning to take shape.

signals.heading: Four current signals on discovering the market through real customer behavior.

fieldNotes.title: Meta brings an AI agent into the small-business stack
fieldNotes.whatHappened: Meta launched Muse for Small Business, an AI agent that can work across business software including Instagram, Facebook, Shopify, Stripe, QuickBooks, Asana, Box, Canva, and Zoom, with human approval available before purchases or publishing.
fieldNotes.whyItMatters: The product is entering the market through an existing operating context rather than asking small businesses to adopt another isolated assistant. The real discovery question is which cross-tool tasks owners repeatedly trust the agent to handle.
fieldNotes.watch: Watch which approved workflows become habitual, and where businesses still require a human handoff before the product definition can expand.

fieldNotes.title: AI referrals are becoming a measurable shopping channel
fieldNotes.whatHappened: Adobe expects AI traffic to U.S. retail sites to more than double this holiday season. In its survey, AI-referred shoppers added items to carts at a 32% higher rate, while 43% generated more revenue per visit than non-AI traffic.
fieldNotes.whyItMatters: The emerging market is not simply AI search; it is a new discovery and referral layer in which brands must be legible to both the shopper and the shopper's assistant. The observed behavior is more useful than a forecast about eventual channel size.
fieldNotes.watch: Watch whether higher cart activity persists through completed purchases, returns, and repeat visits once more autonomous shopping agents enter the path.

fieldNotes.title: Kroger links creative choices to conversion before media spend
fieldNotes.whatHappened: Kroger, Vidmob, and MMA Global used predictive creative scoring across more than 1,900 assets and reported 81% accuracy in forecasting e-commerce conversion; aligned creative averaged a four-times improvement in conversion rates.
fieldNotes.whyItMatters: This is a market-discovery loop for marketing itself: creative attributes become hypotheses, live sales become the evidence, and the next media allocation changes accordingly. The advantage is not merely using AI, but building a proprietary feedback loop around real outcomes.
fieldNotes.watch: Watch whether the predictive signal transfers across audiences and formats, or remains useful only inside the specific campaign context from which it was learned.

fieldNotes.title: ChatGPT tests shopping through try-on and saved intent
fieldNotes.whatHappened: OpenAI launched virtual try-on for clothing and accessories plus Favorites, allowing shoppers to upload a selfie or product image, visualize an item, and save products in a Library for later.
fieldNotes.whyItMatters: The product is probing two concrete behaviors—confidence before purchase and deferred intent—rather than claiming that conversational shopping is already a finished category. Those behaviors can reveal whether visual assistance earns a place in the buying journey.
fieldNotes.watch: Watch whether try-on increases qualified product exploration and eventual conversion, or whether the novelty ends before shoppers make a purchase.

tweets.author: signüll
tweets.title: A product lesson: demonstrate the pain that already exists
tweets.summary: This fragment is useful as a discovery test: an AI product becomes legible when it removes a familiar, repeated annoyance instead of performing a spectacular but rare task.
tweets.text:
there are so many everyday demos that could make ai, personal agents, & agents in general feel insanely powerful to normal ppl & yet ai companies keep choosing things like booking flights, planning travel, or god forbid planning a god damn wedding.

these are not everyday problems. they’re relatively rare events & worse for a lot of ppl they’re actually part of the joys of life. the best demo should make someone feel pain they already are familiar with disappearing. almost every company gets this wrong. they optimize for spectacle instead of relief which is fine in some cases but it doesn’t last.

show me the annoying thing i deal with every single day then make it disappear. it’s not sexy, i guarantee it will work.

signals.tweetHeading: One fragment from the timeline worth carrying into the work.
